title: Fifteen Days of Water
word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
hookLine: a boy fasts and forgets everything he learned. his father feeds him, and it all comes back
carry: the mind is made of food
tomorrow: where does salt go when it disappears in water?
last: HEALTH IS THE ROOT OF DHARMA.

cards: Shvetaketu has just come home after twelve years of study, and he's rather proud of himself. In the Chandogya Upanishad, his father, Uddalaka, decides to teach him what school didn't. First, a strange test.
Don't eat for fifteen days, he says. Drink all the water you like; you won't die, because breath runs on water. Fifteen days later the boy comes back, and his father says: recite the Vedas.
Shvetaketu, who knew them all, stands there. Nothing comes. Sir, he says, they don't come to me.

teach.b: His father explains with a picture. Of a great fire, one ember is left, no bigger than a firefly. It can't burn much.
Feed it straw, and it blazes up again. Go and eat, he says. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and recites everything.

And Uddalaka gives him the line the story was built for: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Hindu tradition takes that seriously. What goes in becomes you, not only the body but the mind you think and pray with.
Later in the same Upanishad: when food is pure, the mind is pure, and when the mind is pure, memory holds firm. Many teachers, Shankara among them, read food there as everything the senses take in.

teach.h: THE MIND IS MADE OF FOOD.
teach.b: It's why the Gita, in its seventeenth chapter, sorts food by the three gunas: fresh, nourishing, sattvic food that brings strength and contentment; burning, harsh, rajasic food that the Gita says brings pain and grief; stale, spoiled food that suits the dull, tamasic temper.
It's why many families offer food to God before they eat it.
Ayurveda has a cousin of that logic in one rule from the Charaka Samhita: for all things, at all times, the similar increases and the unlike decreases. Heat on heat stacks up; heavy on heavy.
On this path that rule is for noticing what's stacking up, never for prescribing a diet, and health questions go to a doctor. And today?
Shvetaketu's ember shows what the night before an exam can forget: you're not only filling a stomach. You're building the mind that has to remember.

how: Many Hindu families offer food to God before eating and receive it as prasad, and some keep simpler, sattvic food on fast days; the Chandogya's 'the mind is made of food' and the Gita's sorting of food by the three gunas stand behind the practice, and Ayurveda's rule that like increases like is used on this path only for noticing.

games.q: what does “the three doshas as a way of noticing” mean?
o: three tests a doctor runs to find an illness
three kinds of food the old texts forbid outright
three forces that grow when like is added to like

p: fasted fifteen days and forgot his Vedas
fed with straw, it blazes again
strength and contentment, in the Gita

s: Uddalaka told his son the mind is made of food
after the fast, Shvetaketu ate and recited everything again.
the Gita says all food is spiritually the same
chapter 17 sorts food by the three gunas: sattvic, rajasic, tamasic.
on this path, Charaka's rule tells you what to eat to cure an illness
it's for noticing what's stacking up. health questions go to a doctor.

games.q: test tomorrow. it's 11pm: a third energy drink, a bag of chips, a phone full of drama. by Uddalaka's line, what are you building?
o: nothing: what goes in has no effect on the mind.
a mind made of rush and noise, since what you take in becomes you.
a sharper memory: more input, more fuel.
games.why: the mind is made of food, and like increases like. when food is pure, the Chandogya says, the mind is pure and memory holds.

practice: At your next meal, if your family offers food first, do it: set the plate down, offer it to God in your heart or with a short prayer you know, then eat it as prasad.
If you don't pray, take the first three bites slowly and really taste them, the way Shvetaketu must have after fifteen days. Either way, notice that you're feeding a mind, not just a body.

wordCard.voice: The three doshas, as a way of noticing. Today, Charaka's rule, like increases like, and the Upanishad's older line underneath it: the mind is made of food.

orig.note: Sanskrit: food. 'annamayam hi somya manah': the mind, my dear, is made of food (Chandogya Upanishad 6.5.4).

carryVoice: Your line: the mind is made of food. Feed the ember well, and it blazes. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1 (Shvetaketu returns after twelve years of study, proud)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.7.1–6 (the fifteen-day fast on water; the Vedas do not come; the ember like a firefly fed with straw; he eats and recites)
Chandogya Upanishad 7.26.2 (when food is pure, the mind is pure; then memory is firm), with Shankara's commentary reading ahara as what the senses take in
Bhagavad Gita 17.8–10 (sattvic, rajasic and tamasic food)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 1.44 (for all things at all times, the similar is the cause of increase and the dissimilar the cause of decrease)
